rules.statement: Any code that issues a JWT addressed to a client (ID token, logout token, UserInfo response, JWT introspection response, or a new kind) must get its signing and encryption credentials from the shared public client JWT credential selector, not choose algorithms or keys itself.
rules.why: There is one policy for protecting a client's JWTs the way the client registered. Code that copies that policy drifts from it, and code that skips it protects tokens more weakly than the client registered.
rules.check: Look for new or changed JWT issuers addressed to a client that pick signing algorithms, signing keys, or client encryption keys directly from client metadata or key stores instead of resolving the credential selector.

rules.statement: A replacement or extension of the client JWT credential selection policy must never return credentials weaker than the client's registered signing and encryption metadata, for example by leaving out encryption or using a different algorithm.
rules.why: Replacements may add selection rules, such as choosing among the client's keys, but they must not weaken the protection the client registered.
rules.check: In custom selector implementations, check for paths that drop encryption, ignore the registered algorithm, or fall back to defaults that differ from the client's registration.

rules.statement: When a policy must be reusable by replaceable public services, expose it as a public interface in the abstractions package, keep the default implementation internal, and register the default only when no other implementation is registered (TryAdd).
rules.why: Making only the concrete class public fixes the policy's dependencies into the public API. Keeping the policy internal forces every replacement to reimplement it. A conditional registration lets deployments replace or extend it.
rules.check: Look for replaceable policies exposed as public concrete classes, default implementations registered with Add instead of TryAdd, or public services whose replacements would need internal-only types to behave the same as the default.

rules.statement: Model a set of kinds or settings that other packages may extend as an open type with well-known static instances, not as a closed enum or switch over a fixed list.
rules.why: Vocabularies are open unless provably closed, so a package that adds a new kind can describe it with a new instance without changing the core.
rules.check: Look for new enums or exhaustive switches that represent extensible kinds, such as token kinds or protection settings, where third-party packages would need to add values.
